weakness: The grasp aimed at one averaged snapshot of the ball's position. When the ball started rolling (4 cm/s) the gripper closed where the ball had been, and every retry re-aimed at a fresh but already stale position, closing on empty space until the ball rolled off the table (0/10). A perception call also threw once on the platform, which crashed that run.
how_found: A1 in assumptions.md: between the detection and the moment the fingers close there are 1-2 s of arm motion, and the scene is explicitly dynamic, so a still target is the first thing a real scene breaks (a nudged or rolling object).
why_missed: In the base task the ball always lay still until touched, so position-only perception was enough and the retry loop looked like robustness; the retry never checked whether the target was still where it had been aimed.
fix: acquire_ball(): estimate the ball's velocity from 6 averaged detections over 0.5 s; if it moves, pre-position the open gripper 2.6 s ahead on its path with the closing axis across the motion, then re-measure in a closed loop and close only when the ball is between the fingers (along-track distance <= speed x close delay, lateral < 3 cm); a still ball must be within 1.5 cm of the finger centre or the attempt aborts upward and retries. Also: detect() failures are caught, and the carry ends with a correcting move to the release point.
general_rule: Before committing to a contact action, estimate the target's velocity (not just its position) and re-verify its pose relative to the end effector immediately before the irreversible step; intercept a moving target at a predicted point with the gripper oriented to receive it, and abort rather than act blind when the check fails.

weakness: The carry moved the held ball 8 cm above the platform top with no obstacle list and no check of the moves' results. Two walls between the ball and the sorter (top 6 cm above the carry height) knocked the ball out of the gripper or stopped the arm; when the long carry move failed to plan, the next (lower) move was executed anyway and dragged the ball through the wall (0/10).
how_found: A6 in assumptions.md: every motion passed no avoid list and the transport height was set only by the target surface, so anything taller than that between pick and place was invisible to the program; clutter on the path is the commonest real-world difference.
why_missed: The base scene had nothing between the ball and the sorter and the planner always avoided the table, so collision-free paths came for free; I also treated a failed move as harmless and carried on with the next waypoint.
fix: Perceive obstacles (get_obstacles averaged over 10 calls) and pass them to every motion; raise the carry height so the held ball's bottom clears the top of any obstacle near the pick-to-place corridor by 3.5 cm (the planner models the arm, not the held object); move the ball by its own centre (move_ball_to) and, when a plan fails, retry with the gripper turned about the vertical (a sphere's grasp yaw is free) or via a higher midpoint, and stop instead of continuing low if all fail; try every top-down grasp candidate until one whose approach and straight descent both plan.
general_rule: Size every transport waypoint to the swept volume of the arm plus the held object (the planner usually models only the arm), pass perceived obstacles to every plan, and treat a failed motion as a stop condition that triggers an alternative, never as a step to skip.

weakness: The release point was hard-coded as the point of the hole's orbit on the working arm's own side. Two brackets hanging over the sorter on both sides (3 cm thick, 7 cm above the platform) left that point unreachable at the release height; the arm stopped above the bracket and opened there, so the ball landed on the bracket or the solid platform (0/10).
how_found: A5/A13: P = centre + side * [r, 0] was a convenience choice, not a requirement; the goal only needs the ball to meet the hole, which passes under every point of its orbit once per revolution. A fixed place pose is exactly what a fixture or clamp near the goal invalidates.
why_missed: The first free choice worked, so I never wrote down that it was a choice; the set of equivalent goal poses was collapsed to one point in the code.
fix: release_point(): enumerate points of the hole's orbit (every 15 deg, starting from the arm's side and turning towards the robot first) and take the first whose vertical column (gripper radius 4.5 cm, 35 cm above the platform) is free of perceived obstacles; the timing solver already works for any orbit angle.
general_rule: When the goal admits a family of equivalent target poses (any point on a path, any angle about a symmetry axis), keep the whole family in the program and choose a member at run time by checking it against the perceived free space, instead of hard-coding the first one that worked.

weakness: Grasp orientation was whatever the candidate generator ranked first (fingers along world x). With a box 6 mm beside the ball on that axis, an open finger came down on the box: the ball was pushed or the arm stopped, and the 'still, off-centre' check then retried into the same collision (s_break 0.3). After the fix forced the fingers along y, a second, hidden weakness appeared: at release the fingers stood tangentially to the hole's motion, and a ball sinking into the moving hole was carried into an open fingertip and lifted back onto the platform (stuck). The release also had a systematic ~45 ms lag and a few-mm radial placement error.
how_found: A11/A14: the space around the target was never checked against the gripper, only the arm path against the planner; v2 had already shown that the planner does not model the gripper body. Ground-truth logs of failed episodes then showed the ball still touching a finger (held=True) when it stuck, after a clean landing over the hole.
why_missed: In the base scene the ball is alone and the default finger axis happened to be radial at the release point, so neither the grasp footprint nor the finger orientation at release ever mattered.
fix: Rank grasp candidates by the xy clearance of both open fingertips (centre +- 6 cm along the closing axis) to perceived obstacle footprints; before release turn the gripper about the vertical so the closing axis is radial (fingers out of the hole's tangential path); release higher (ball bottom 5.5 cm above the platform, fingertips clear of a ball sitting in the hole) with LEAD = 0.465 s + free-fall time computed from the height; correct the release position up to 3 times to within 2 mm.
general_rule: Check the gripper's own footprint (open fingertips, not just the planned arm) against neighbouring objects when choosing a grasp, and at release orient and retract the fingers so they are outside the region the released object will move through.

weakness: Two boxes beside the ball (on its +x and -y sides) blocked all four precomputed top-down grasp yaws, so the open fingers landed on a box every time (s_break 0.1). Generating extra yaws (every 15 deg, ranked by fingertip clearance) fixed the grasp at once in the probe, but the full check never reached 0.8 on every scene: the last four --all runs gave min 0.6-0.7, with base 0.9-1.0 and each variation fluctuating between 0.5 and 0.9 from run to run with identical code. Almost all remaining failures were 'ball stuck on platform': the timed drop through a hole only 5 mm wider than the ball.
how_found: Same assumption family as v4 (labelled parameter_tuning): v4's fix only chose among the four candidates the generator returned, so I asked what happens when none of them is clear.
why_missed: Not a design miss for the grasp (the fix was one function). The repair failed on a different, underlying weakness that v4 had already exposed: the drop's end-to-end error (release delay jitter ~+-20 ms = +-4 mm at the hole's 0.2 m/s, plus a 3-6 mm sideways push from the opening fingers whose direction depends on the gripper yaw) is about the size of the 5 mm clearance, so success per episode is ~0.75-0.85 and a 10-seed estimate swings +-0.15. I ran 4 of the 6 allowed repair iterations through the full check (extra yaws; a higher release with free-fall-derived timing plus never opening when the release pose was not reached; aiming 4-6 mm inside the orbit; landing 10 mm upstream of the hole) and tried a lighter grip before release in the probe only (it released the ball early), then stopped because no lever moved the release error below the clearance; per-seed ground truth showed the ball still sometimes resting on the rim with a centre error of only 4-6 mm.
fix: None kept: v5 marked unsolved and reverted; pipeline.py is the round-4 version (the v5 attempt is saved as dev/pipeline_v5_attempt.py).
general_rule: When success hinges on a tolerance near the noise floor, measure the full distribution of the actuation error (timing jitter and the displacement the actuator itself adds) on repeated trials before tuning means, and change the strategy (more margin, a closed-loop correction, or a second chance) when the tolerance is under about three standard deviations, because no single calibrated constant will make it reliable.
